title: Supreme Court Sets Seven-Day Deadline for Aid to Rescued Bonded Labourers
meta_description: Supreme Court directs nationwide timelines for release certificates and rehabilitation aid to bonded labourers, holding delay can amount to denial.
bench: Vikram Nath and Aparesh Kumar Singh, JJ.
case_name: Surendra Manjhi & Anr. v. Union of India & Ors.
body: On 2 November 2026, the Supreme Court, in a judgment delivered by Justices Vikram Nath and Aparesh Kumar Singh, laid down a nationwide timeline for how quickly a rescued bonded labourer must receive a release certificate and financial help. The ruling, in Surendra Manjhi & Anr. v. Union of India & Ors. (2026 INSC 1185), grew out of a writ petition filed under Article 32 of the Constitution by a survivor who had waited years for the assistance the law promised him.

Manjhi was among a group rescued from a brick kiln in Shahjahanpur district, Uttar Pradesh, on 28 February 2019. After the rescue, he was sent back to his home state, Bihar, and issued a release certificate recognising him as a former bonded labourer. The financial assistance due to him under the Central Sector Scheme for Rehabilitation of Bonded Labourers did not arrive until 2022, nearly three years after he had already been identified and certified as rescued.

That gap, between the paperwork confirming his rescue and the money actually reaching him, became the heart of the case. During the proceedings, the Court had already directed the Union government to work out, together with the States, Union Territories and the National Human Rights Commission, a simpler procedure for issuing release certificates and disbursing financial aid quickly. The Union responded with a compliance affidavit and a revised Standard Operating Procedure dated 14 May 2026, which the Court has now made binding across the country.

The bench held that a State's duty towards a bonded labourer does not end the moment he is physically freed. Identification, release and rehabilitation, the Court said, are three stages of a single constitutional obligation under Article 23, and treating rescue as the finish line lets rehabilitation drift indefinitely while the survivor is left without support. Delay in rehabilitation, the judgment observed, can in substance amount to its denial.

To close that gap, the Court fixed specific outer limits. Once an authority determines that a person has in fact been held in bondage, it must ordinarily issue the release certificate within twenty-four hours of that finding. Immediate financial assistance must then ordinarily follow within seven days of the certificate, subject to the verification the scheme requires. The Court also directed the Union to prescribe one release certificate format for every State and Union Territory to use, instead of the patchwork of formats that had allowed delays to creep in at the paperwork stage, and to make the NAVJIVAN portal work as the single record for tracking a survivor's progress from rescue through to rehabilitation.

The Court rejected any suggestion that this assistance should wait for a criminal trial against those who held the survivor in bondage to run its course. Prosecution and rehabilitation, it held, are separate tracks, and a survivor's immediate relief cannot be made to depend on how long a criminal case takes. The Union was also directed to decide, within three months, whether the amount of financial assistance and the scheme itself need revising, and to file a compliance affidavit within four months confirming what has actually changed on the ground. The petition stays open, listed again after seven months so the Court can check whether its directions are being followed rather than filed away.

The Bonded Labour System (Abolition) Act, 1976, which the petition sought to enforce, was itself passed to give effect to Article 23 of the Constitution, which prohibits forced labour and traffic in human beings. Courts have long treated that prohibition as one of the few fundamental rights enforceable directly against private individuals, beyond the State alone, which is why rescue operations typically involve a mix of police, the district administration and labour officials acting together under the Act, rather than a single department working alone.

For state governments and labour departments, the order converts what had been a scheme implemented at varying speed into fixed deadlines, with the Supreme Court itself tracking compliance. For survivors and the organisations that work with them, it gives a concrete number, seven days, to point to when assistance is late, instead of arguing over what counts as reasonable time. A rescue that used to end, in practice, with a certificate and a long wait now carries a clock the authorities cannot ignore without inviting the Court's attention at the next compliance check.
why_it_matters: The ruling turns what used to be a loosely monitored welfare scheme into fixed deadlines that every State and Union Territory must follow: a release certificate within a day of identification, and financial assistance within a week of that certificate. Employers in sectors such as brick kilns, construction and agriculture, where bonded or forced labour risk is highest, should expect faster identification and documentation once a case surfaces, and closer scrutiny of labour practices generally, since the Court has made the Union directly accountable for uniform, time-bound compliance across the country.
card_summary: Supreme Court fixes nationwide deadlines, 24 hours for a release certificate and 7 days for financial aid, for rehabilitating rescued bonded labourers, holding delay can amount to denial of their rights.
card_tip: Assuming a bonded labour rescue ends once the worker is freed. The Supreme Court has now made release certificates and aid time-bound, enforceable obligations on the State.
verification_notes: AUDIENCE: domestic / general public interest, with compliance relevance for employers in high-risk sectors. TARGET QUERY: what happens after a bonded labourer is rescued in India, how soon should compensation arrive. DEMAND EVIDENCE: none seen (no search-volume or trending data was available; topic chosen for its freshness, significance and fit within the firm's employment and labour practice area). Bench, citation, date, background facts (Shahjahanpur rescue on 28 February 2019, repatriation to Bihar, disbursal only in 2022) and the specific directions (24-hour certificate, 7-day assistance, SOP dated 14 May 2026, NAVJIVAN portal, 3-month and 4-month compliance deadlines) confirmed across Verdictum, LiveLaw, Lawchakra and Courtbook, which describe the directions in consistent terms. Left out: the exact number of persons rescued alongside Manjhi and the identity of the kiln's operators, since sources did not specify these; the current enhancement amount under the Central Sector Scheme, since no figure was confirmed from two independent reports.
